03
THE WORKING METHOD
Give the task a destination
An effective prompt begins with an observable outcome.
Build the habit
A vague request produces a vague target. Before asking AI to help, decide what the reader should
understand or do. An email that requests approval, a meeting record that assigns work, and a
summary that supports a decision need different structures. State the deliverable in one sentence
before supplying background. That sentence keeps the output connected to the work instead of
drifting into general advice. Build a brief with five parts: task, audience, source facts, constraints,
and output format. Add a sixth part when accuracy matters: the checks the answer must pass. For
a supplier email, that might mean preserving an order number, marking an unconfirmed delivery
date, and requesting a response without promising compensation.
Try this brief
Draft a 120-word supplier email requesting an updated delivery estimate. Use only the
notes below. Separate confirmed facts from unknowns. Include a subject, the requested
action, and questions for me outside the email. Do not promise a refund or a replacement.
When the first answer misses
Name the defect and change one instruction. Say "Keep the delivery date marked unconfirmed"
rather than "make it better." If the input itself is missing a crucial fact, get that fact from the
responsible person. Repeated prompting cannot create evidence that was never supplied.

03
THE FIVE-STEP IDEA PATH
Notice the moment worth changing
A useful idea begins with attention.
Build the habit
Start with a scene, not a slogan. "People need inspiration" is too broad to investigate. "A new team
member has three links and cannot tell which instruction is current" gives you a person, a task, and
a point of friction. Record what happened, what the person tried, and what stopped them. Keep
your interpretation beside the observation instead of mixing them together.
An observation can come from your own work, a voluntary conversation, or a process you have
permission to watch. Ask about the last actual occasion. What triggered the task? What happened
next? Which workaround helped? A story about yesterday usually gives you more usable detail
than a prediction about an imaginary future product.
Keep the spark honest
Fictional observation: a club organizer sent the same location directions to four people
before one event. Interpretation: the invitation may be hard to navigate. Possible response:
a clearer event card. The observation supports investigation; it does not establish that
anyone wants another app.
Turn attention into a brief
Write one sentence that names the person, situation, and desired improvement. Then record the
evidence you have and the question you still need answered. Collect alternatives before
committing to a solution. A better invitation, a confirmation message, and a map link may address
the same friction at very different costs. Choose a problem small enough to examine this week and
meaningful enough that solving it would matter.

Keep four evidence labels distinct
SOURCE-CONFIRMED means the cited source supports the stated claim within its scope.
LOCALLY VERIFIED requires your own recorded test. DESIGN OPTION identifies an
original proposal in this guide. UNVERIFIED identifies a dependency the research has not
established. No prototype or application design here should be assumed production-ready.

01 / OWNERSHIP AND VALUE
Read the asset in layers
The token, the media, and the promise are different objects.
Understand the mechanism
Begin by separating the ledger record from everything attached to it. A record may identify an item
and its current controller. Metadata describes the item. Media supplies the image, audio, or
animation. A license states permitted uses. An application delivers benefits. A support process
handles exceptions. The buyer encounters one product, but the operator must maintain several
distinct systems.
This separation changes the questions you ask. A token transfer does not automatically transfer a
physical parcel, a copyright, or a subscription account. A media file can remain available after a
membership ends. A service can close while its historical token record remains visible. Investigate
each layer rather than allowing the word ownership to stand in for every possible right.
A collectible is a bundle of dependencies
Illustrative item: character 014 includes a downloadable portrait and access to a hosted
animation. The portrait may remain usable if the application closes, while the animation
may not. The terms should explain that difference before purchase. A ledger entry alone
cannot deliver the animation or maintain the hosting account.
Build a promise inventory
Write each promised benefit beside its responsible system, owner, duration, and failure response.
Identify what the customer can retain independently and what requires continued service. Treat a
missing answer as a design decision to resolve, not as wording to hide. This inventory is the
foundation for the architecture, the cost model, and the product page. If two teams use ownership
differently, reconcile their definitions before implementation begins.
